parole.significato: A type of spicy, spreadable salami from Calabria.

parole.significato: Kidney.

parole.significato: Urine.

parole.significato: Any of a set of signs used in early musical notation.
parole.testo: From 15th c. Middle English newme, nevme, neme; from Middle French neume, in turn from Medieval Latin neuma or pneuma, either from Ancient Greek νεῦμα (neûma, “sign”), or else a corruption of πνεῦμα (pneûma, “breath”). In the latter case a doublet of pneuma.

parole.significato: Neutral; on neither side; neither one thing nor another.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English neutre, from Latin neuter, from ne (“not”) + uter (“either”), a semantic loan from Koine Greek οὐδέτερος (oudéteros); compare English either, English whether, and neither.

parole.significato: Either of two kinds of supporting post in a staircase.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English nowel, *newel, from Old French noel, from either Early Medieval Latin nōdellus (“buckle”, diminutive of nōdus "knot") or Late Latin nucālis (“nut-like”, derivative of nux "nut"). Doublet of noil and noyau.

parole.significato: A short fibre left over from combing wool or spinning silk during the preparation of textile yarns.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English *noyel, from Old French noiel, variant of noel, from either Early Medieval Latin nōdellus (“buckle”, diminutive of nōdus "knot") or Late Latin nucālis (“nut-like”, derivative of nux "nut"). Doublet of newel and noyau.

parole.significato: Various sounds, usually unwanted or unpleasant.
parole.testo: From Middle English noyse, noise, from Old French noise (“a dispute, wrangle, strife, noise”), of uncertain origin. parole.significato: A pseudonym used in online communications; a handle.
parole.testo: Pseudo-Gallicism, derived from nom (“name”) + de (“of”) + clavier (“keyboard”), by analogy with nom de plume.

parole.significato: A pseudonym used when publishing on the World Wide Web.
parole.testo: Pseudo-Gallicism, derived from nom (“name”) + de (“of”) + Web, by analogy with nom de guerre.

parole.significato: Synonym of ninetysomething: a person between 90 and 99 years old.
parole.testo: From Latin nōnāgēnārius (“containing ninety”) + -an (suffix forming adjectives and representative nouns), either directly or via French nonagénaire, from nōnāgēnī (“ninety each”) + -ārius (“-ary”), from nōnāginta (“nine tens, ninety”).

parole.significato: Of or related to the number ninety.
parole.testo: From Latin nōnāgēnārius (“containing 90”) either directly or via Middle French nonagénaire, from Latin nōnāgēnī (“90 each”) + -ārius (“-ary”), from nōnāgintā (“nine tens, 90”).

parole.significato: To hum or sing (a tune) at a low pitch or volume.
parole.testo: Possibly either: * a blend of Shetland Scots nune (“to sing softly, croon, hum”) (from Danish nynne, Norwegian nuna, nynna (“to hum; to sing”), originally imitative) + English doodle (“to play the bagpipes”) (chiefly Scotland); or * from Norn (unattested), from Old Norse *grynta, from Proto-Germanic

parole.significato: An act of putting a person in a headlock and rubbing one's knuckles on the other person's head, often a playful gesture…
parole.testo: Unknown, possibly from Yiddish נודזשען (nudzhen, “to badger”), or possibly from Hebrew נוגות (nugot, “afflict”) (see Eicha/Lamentations 1:3) or possibly via an alteration of nudge, matching the alteration of wedge to wedgie.

parole.significato: An adjustable loop of rope, such as the one placed around the neck in hangings, or the one at the end of a lasso.
parole.testo: From Middle English nose (“noose, loop”), of unclear origin. parole.significato: A novice.
parole.testo: First attested in 1517; either borrowed from Middle French noviciat, novitiat or from Medieval Latin noviciātus, novitiātus (“a novitiate”), from Latin novicius, novitius + -ātus (see -ate (forming nouns denoting a rank or office)), from novus (“new”). Sense 1 is not attested in cognates.

parole.significato: A French liqueur made at Poissy in north central France from brandy and flavoured with almonds and the pits of apricots.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French noyau, from Middle French noyau, from Old French noel, from either Early Medieval Latin nōdellus (“buckle”) or Late Latin nucālis (“nut-like”). Doublet of newel and noil.

parole.significato: The innermost section of a chrysalis in a silk cocoon.
parole.testo: Either directly from Middle Low German, or from knub, from a Middle Low German word (compare Low German Knubbel, Knobbel (“knot; lump”)). Compare knob.

parole.significato: The most important of a group.
parole.testo: From either Spanish número uno or Italian numero uno. Piecewise doublet of number one.

parole.significato: Of or relating to a numen (divinity); indicating the presence of a divinity.
parole.testo: From Latin nūmen (“nod of the head; divine sway or will; divinity”) + -ous (suffix forming adjectives from nouns, denoting possession or presence of a quality). parole.significato: Caligavis obscura, a honeyeater species found in New Guinea.
parole.testo: From obscure + honeyeater, a partial calque from translingual of either translingual Meliphaga obscura, translingual Lichenostomus obscurus or translingual Caligavis obscura.

parole.significato: eight
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ὀκτώ (oktṓ, “eight”) and Latin octō (“eight”).

parole.significato: Synonym of eightysomething: a person between 80 and 89 years old.
parole.testo: From Latin octōgēnārius + -an (suffix forming adjectives and representative nouns), either directly or via French octogénaire, from Latin octōgēnus (“80 each”) + -ārius (“-ary”), from octōgintā (“eight tens, 80”).

parole.significato: Of or related to the number 80, particularly
parole.testo: From Latin octōgēnārius (“containing 80”) either directly or via French octogénaire, from Latin octōgēnus (“80 each”) + -ārius (“-ary”), from octōgintā (“eight tens, 80”). Cognate with octogenarian.

parole.significato: To stare at (someone or something), especially impertinently, amorously, or covetously.
parole.testo: 17th century. parole.significato: Additional costs; extra expenses.
parole.testo: From on- + cost, or from Middle English uncost (“additional expense”), from Middle Dutch oncost (“expenses, overhead”) (Modern Dutch onkost), equivalent to un- + cost. Cognate with German Unkosten (“expenses”).

parole.significato: A partially fermented tea, often roasted, which combines the characteristics of green tea and black tea.
parole.testo: 1850s. From either Mandarin 烏龍 /乌龙 (wūlóng) due to hypercorrection, or directly from Hokkien 烏龍 /乌龙 (o͘-liông), from 烏 /乌 (o͘, “black”) + 龍 /龙 (liông, “dragon”). See also pouchong from Hokkien 包種茶 /包种茶 (pau-chióng-tê, literally “tea of the wrapped kind”).

parole.significato: A yellow-brown, addictive narcotic drug obtained from the dried juice of unripe pods of the opium poppy, Papaver somnif…

parole.testo: From Old French (also modern) orle, from orler (“to hem”), or from Vulgar Latin *orula, a diminutive of Latin ora (“edge”), probably from os, oris (“mouth”).

parole.significato: A white person.

parole.testo: Uncertain. Borrowed from French, either from the Sahaptin name of the Palus people or a designation of the region as pelouse.

parole.testo: Apparently from para- + -gnath + -a, after either German Paragnathen pl or French paragnathes pl. Compare later paragnath and paragnathus.

parole.significato: To afflict with paralysis.
parole.testo: Partly a borrowing from French. Probably partly either (i) formed within English, by derivation. Or partly (ii) a borrowing from French, combined with an English element. Etymons: Middle English paralysie, -ize suffix; French paralyser.

parole.significato: A play or a musical product which has a pastoral subject.
parole.testo: From French, from Middle French pastorale; or from Italian pastorale, hence the plural pastorali.

parole.significato: The head, particularly the top or crown.
parole.testo: From Middle English pate, of uncertain origin. Perhaps a shortened form of Old French patene or Medieval Latin patena, both from Latin patina (“pan, dish”). Alternatively, perhaps akin to Old Frisian pote (“skull”).

parole.significato: A paved outside area, adjoining a house, used for dining or recreation.
parole.testo: From Spanish patio, either from Old Occitan patu or pati (compare Occitan and Catalan pati), of uncertain origin.

parole.significato: To act as a patron of; to defend, protect, or support.
parole.testo: From patron + -ize (verb ending); or from Old French patroniser, from Medieval Latin patronizāre (“to lead a galley as patron”). Piecewise doublet of patternize.

parole.testo: 17th c., perhaps from Low German or Dutch pal (“catch (mechanism)”), or from either French pal (“stake”) or épaule (“shoulder”).

parole.significato: Relating to the Pawnee people or language.
parole.testo: Borrowing from French Pani, from Algonquin pani, either from Winnebago pa꞉ní or Chiwere pányi.

parole.significato: Any of several types of trees having edible fruit
parole.testo: Via Portuguese and Spanish papaya from Lokono papáia; compare also Kari'na kapaja. Doublet of papaya. Alternatively from Yuchi pahpah.

parole.significato: pederasty
parole.testo: Probably either the post-Classical Latin paederastia or its etymon, the Ancient Greek παιδερᾰστίᾱ (paiderăstíā), suffixed with the English -ice (suffix forming abstract nouns). Compare pederasty.

parole.significato: Alternative form of pelta.
parole.testo: A variant of pelta, borrowed from Latin pelta, from Ancient Greek πέλτη (péltē, “small crescent-shaped leather shield of Thracian design”); further etymology uncertain, perhaps either from Thracian, or ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *pel- (“to cover; to wrap; hide; skin; cloth”).

parole.significato: To write (something) using a pencil.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman and Old French pincil (see the variant pincel, which gave rise to Modern French pinceau (“paintbrush”)), from Latin pēnicillum, diminutive of pēniculus (“brush”), itself a diminutive of pēnis (“tail; penis”). Doublet of penis. Not related to pen.

parole.significato: In verbs: denoting the sense "through", as in perforate.
